scenes.text: How to evaluate a casino game aggregator, before you sign. Seven questions you can answer yourself, without a single sales call.

Most operators who start comparing aggregators are not unhappy. A contract is up for renewal, a new brand has a different shape, a new market changes the content you need. Benchmarking is healthy. Start with the question that decides everything else: are you buying a content layer, or a whole platform? Comparing a bundled suite against a pure aggregation API, without saying so, is how procurement goes wrong.

One. Catalog fit, not catalog size. Whether the game providers your market actually plays are licensed in your jurisdictions matters far more than any headline number on a homepage. Two. The integration model. Be explicit about what you are buying. Three. Documentation you can read today. Vague docs before a contract rarely improve after one.

Four. Wallet semantics. Ask precisely how duplicate transaction I Ds, rollbacks, timeouts and disconnected rounds are handled. This is where integrations hurt, months later. Five. Reporting granularity. Per-game, per-provider and per-player reporting, close to real time, with exports your B I stack can read without manual work.

Six. Commercial flexibility. Contract length, minimums, revenue-share structure, and what happens if a market closes. Flexibility at signature is easier to get than flexibility at renewal. Seven. Exit cost. The more of your stack sits with one vendor, the harder a future migration becomes. Decide deliberately how much you consolidate.

Whichever names end up on your shortlist, judge them all the same way. We would rather you tested the shortlist than took our word for it. Book a walkthrough with our team at iplaygames dot A I. iPlay Games.
